plain_english: Why do you agree with something? Because it seems true to you. You can't agree with something that seems false. Why not? Because your mind naturally leans toward truth. It rejects what's false. When uncertain, it holds back judgment. Want proof? Try to convince yourself it's nighttime right now. You can't. Try to stop believing it's daytime. You can't. Try to believe the stars are an even number. Impossible. So when someone believes something false, know this: they didn't mean to believe a lie. No one willingly gives up truth, as Plato said. The false thing just looked true to them.
original_excerpt: What is the cause of assenting to anything? The fact that it appears to be true. It is not possible then to assent to that which appears not to be true. Why? Because this is the nature of the understanding, to incline to the true, to be dissatisfied with the false, and in matters uncertain to withhold assent. What is the proof of this? Imagine (persuade yourself), if you can, that it is now night. It is not possible. Take away your persuasion that it is day. It is not possible. Persuade yourself or take away your persuasion that the stars are even in number. It is impossible. When then any man assents to that which is false, be assured that he did not intend to assent to it as false, for every soul is unwillingly deprived of the truth, as Plato says; but the falsity seemed to him to be true.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Angry with Men; and What Are the Small and the Great Things Among Men, Section 1

plain_english:
In actions, we have something similar to truth and falsehood. We have what's right and wrong, what's helpful and harmful, what fits a person and what doesn't. Can someone think something is useful and then not choose it? No. They can't. Look at what Medea says:

"I know the evil I'm about to do, But passion overpowers my better judgment."

She thought revenge on her husband would benefit her more than sparing her children. That's how it seemed to her — but she was wrong. Show her clearly that she's wrong, and she won't do it. But as long as you don't show her, what else can she follow except what seems right to her? Nothing else. So why are you angry with this miserable woman for being confused about the most important things? Why has she become a monster instead of staying human? Why not pity her instead — the way we pity the blind and the lame? She's blind and crippled in the most important abilities of all.
original_excerpt:
Well, in acts what have we of the like kind as we have here truth or falsehood? We have the fit and the not fit (duty and not duty), the profitable and the unprofitable, that which is suitable to a person and that which is not, and whatever is like these. Can then a man think that a thing is useful to him and not choose it? He cannot. How says Medea?

"'Tis true I know what evil I shall do, But passion overpowers the better counsel."

She thought that to indulge her passion and take vengeance on her husband was more profitable than to spare her children. It was so; but she was deceived. Show her plainly that she is deceived, and she will not do it; but so long as you do not show it, what can she follow except that which appears to herself (her opinion)? Nothing else. Why then are you angry with the unhappy woman that she has been bewildered about the most important things, and is become a viper instead of a human creature? And why not, if it is possible, rather pity, as we pity the blind and the lame, so those who are blinded and maimed in the faculties which are supreme?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Angry with Men; and What Are the Small and the Great Things Among Men, Section 1

plain_english: Remember this clearly: every person acts based on how things appear to them. If something seems good to them, you can't blame them for acting on it. If it seems bad, they're the ones who suffer for their mistake. The person who gets it wrong and the person who pays for it are the same person. If you truly remember this, you won't get angry at anyone. You won't get annoyed or insult anyone. You won't blame or hate anyone. You won't pick fights.
original_excerpt: Whoever then clearly remembers this, that to man the measure of every act is the appearance (the opinion), whether the thing appears good or bad. If good, he is free from blame; if bad, himself suffers the penalty, for it is impossible that he who is deceived can be one person, and he who suffers another person—whoever remembers this will not be angry with any man, will not be vexed at any man, will not revile or blame any man, nor hate, nor quarrel with any man.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Angry with Men; and What Are the Small and the Great Things Among Men, Section 1

plain_english: So all these great and terrible events come from one thing: how we see things. Yes, that's the only source. The entire Iliad is nothing but opinions and how people acted on those opinions. Alexander thought it was good to steal Menelaus's wife. Helen thought it was good to go with him. But what if Menelaus had thought losing such a wife was actually a blessing? What would have happened then? We wouldn't just lose the Iliad — we'd lose the Odyssey too. Did such massive events really depend on something so small? But what do you mean by "massive events"? Wars, civil wars, many men and cities destroyed. And is this such a big deal? Is it nothing? Well, what's the big deal when many cattle die, or many sheep, or when many nests of swallows and storks get burned and destroyed? Are human events like animal events? Very much alike. Human bodies get destroyed, just like cattle and sheep bodies. Human homes burn down, just like stork nests. What's so great or terrible about this? Show me the difference between a human house and a stork's nest — they're both just places to live. The only difference is that humans build their little houses from wood, tiles, and bricks. Storks build theirs from sticks and mud. So are storks and humans alike? What do you think? In terms of their bodies, they're very similar.
original_excerpt: So then all these great and dreadful deeds have this origin, in the appearance (opinion)? Yes, this origin and no other. The Iliad is nothing else than appearance and the use of appearances. It appeared to Alexander to carry off the wife of Menelaus. It appeared to Helene to follow him. If then it had appeared to Menelaus to feel that it was a gain to be deprived of such a wife, what would have happened? Not only would the Iliad have been lost, but the Odyssey also. On so small a matter then did such great things depend? But what do you mean by such great things? Wars and civil commotions, and the destruction of many men and cities. And what great matter is this? Is it nothing? But what great matter is the death of many oxen, and many sheep, and many nests of swallows or storks being burnt or destroyed? Are these things then like those? Very like. Bodies of men are destroyed, and the bodies of oxen and sheep; the dwellings of men are burnt, and the nests of storks. What is there in this great or dreadful? Or show me what is the difference between a man's house and a stork's nest, as far as each is a dwelling; except that man builds his little houses of beams and tiles and bricks, and the stork builds them of sticks and mud. Are a stork and a man then like things? What say you? In body they are very much alike.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Angry with Men; and What Are the Small and the Great Things Among Men, Section 1

plain_english: Does a man differ from a stork in any way? Don't think I'm saying no. But there's no difference in the things I just mentioned. So where is the difference? Look for it and you'll find it somewhere else. See if it's not in a man's understanding of what he does. See if it's not in living with others, in loyalty, in modesty, in steadfastness, in intelligence. So where do you find the great good and evil in people? Right where the difference is. If that difference stays protected and secure — if modesty isn't destroyed, or loyalty, or intelligence — then the man is preserved too. But if any of these gets destroyed and overrun like a conquered city, then the man dies too. That's where the big things happen. You say Alexander suffered great damage when the Greeks invaded and destroyed Troy, and when his brothers died. Not at all. No one gets damaged by something that isn't his own action. What happened then was just the destruction of stork's nests. Alexander's real ruin came when he lost his modesty, loyalty, respect for hospitality, and decency. When was Achilles ruined? Was it when Patroclus died? No. It happened when he started getting angry, when he cried over a girl, when he forgot he was at Troy to fight, not to chase women. These things ruin people. This is what being under siege means. This is how cities get destroyed — when right thinking gets destroyed, when it gets corrupted.
original_excerpt: Does a man then differ in no respect from a stork? Don't suppose that I say so; but there is no difference in these matters (which I have mentioned). In what then is the difference? Seek and you will find that there is a difference in another matter. See whether it is not in a man the understanding of what he does, see if it is not in social community, in fidelity, in modesty, in steadfastness, in intelligence. Where then is the great good and evil in men? It is where the difference is. If the difference is preserved and remains fenced round, and neither modesty is destroyed, nor fidelity, nor intelligence, then the man also is preserved; but if any of these things is destroyed and stormed like a city, then the man too perishes: and in this consist the great things. Alexander, you say, sustained great damage then when the Hellenes invaded and when they ravaged Troy, and when his brothers perished. By no means; for no man is damaged by an action which is not his own; but what happened at that time was only the destruction of stork's nests. Now the ruin of Alexander was when he lost the character of modesty, fidelity, regard to hospitality, and to decency. When was Achilles ruined? Was it when Patroclus died? Not so. But it happened when he began to be angry, when he wept for a girl, when he forgot that he was at Troy not to get mistresses, but to fight. These things are the ruin of men, this is being besieged, this is the destruction of cities, when right opinions are destroyed, when they are corrupted.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought not to Be Angry with Men; and What Are the Small and the Great Things Among Men, Section 1
